You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

I have sleep apnea. My friend sent me this article that contains a promising medication that could help me with sleep apnea and weight loss. Explain the connection between the mentioned medication and sleep apnea and the benefits it may include. Use at least 400 words.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Tirzepatide Significantly Reduces Sleep Disruptions
     2	 Alicia Ault
     3	
     4	
     5	 June 22, 2024
     6	
     7	
     8	 Add to Email Alerts
     9	 28
    10	 2407
    11	
    12	
    13	
    14	 ORLANDO, Fla. — The diabetes and weight loss drug tirzepatide (Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes;
    15	Zepbound for obesity) was so effective at reducing sleep disruptions in patients with obesity and
    16	obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) that 40% to 50% no longer needed to use a continuous pressure airway
    17	positive (CPAP) device, according to two new studies.
    18	
    19	
    20	 Tirzepatide, a long-acting glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist and
    21	glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, also lowered C-reactive protein levels and
    22	systolic blood pressure. And patients taking the medication lost 18% to 20% of their body weight.
    23	
    24	
    25	 The SURMOUNT-OSA studies "mark a significant milestone in the treatment of OSA, offering a
    26	promising new therapeutic option that addresses both respiratory and metabolic complications," said
    27	lead author Atul Malhotra, MD, professor of medicine at University of California San Diego School of
    28	Medicine and director of sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health.
    29	
    30	
    31	 The two double-blind randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity and moderate-to-severe
    32	OSA were conducted at 60 sites in nine countries. The results were presented here at the American
    33	Diabetes Association (ADA) 84th Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published online in the New
    34	England Journal of Medicine.
    35	
    36	
    37	 OSA affects 1 billion people worldwide and 30 million American adults, many of whom are
    38	undiagnosed. Obesity is a common risk factor. According to the ADA, 40% of those with obesity have
    39	OSA and 70% of those with OSA have obesity.
    40	 CPAP is an effective and the most-used intervention for OSA, but many patients refuse to use the
    41	device, stop using it, or cannot use it. Should tirzepatide eventually gain US Food and Drug
    42	Administration (FDA) approval for OSA, it would be the first drug approved for the condition.
    43	
    44	
    45	 "This new drug treatment offers a more accessible alternative for individuals who cannot tolerate
    46	or adhere to existing therapies," said Malhotra.
    47	
    48	
    49	 Huge Reduction in Episodes, Severity
    50	 For the two studies, patients were enrolled who had moderate-to-severe OSA, defined as more than 15
    51	events per hour (using the apnea–hypopnea index [AHI]) and a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or greater.
    52	Those not using a CPAP device were enrolled in study 1, and those using a CPAP device were enrolled
    53	in study 2.
    54	
    55	
    56	 Participants received either the maximum tolerated dose of tirzepatide (10 or 15 mg by once-weekly
    57	injection) or placebo for 1 year. In study 1, 114 individuals received tirzepatide and 120 received
    58	placebo. For study 2, 119 patients received tirzepatide and 114 received placebo. All participants
    59	received regular lifestyle counseling sessions about nutrition and were instructed to reduce food
    60	intake by 500 kcal/day and to engage in at least 150 min/week of physical activity.
    61	
    62	
    63	 Enrollment was limited to 70% men to ensure adequate representation of women.
    64	
    65	
    66	 At baseline, 65% to 70% of participants had severe OSA, with more than 30 events/hour on the AHI
    67	scale and a mean of 51.5 events/hour
    68	
    69	
    70	 By 1 year, patients taking tirzepatide had 27 to 30 fewer events/hour compared with 4 to 6 fewer
    71	events/hour for those taking placebo.
    72	
    73	
    74	 Up to half of those who received tirzepatide in both trials had less than 5 events/hour or 5 to 14
    75	AHI events/hour and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 10 or less. Those thresholds "represent a
    76	level at which CPAP therapy may not be recommended," write the authors.
    77	
    78	
    79	 Patients in the tirzepatide group also had a decrease in systolic blood pressure from baseline of
    80	9.7 mm Hg in study 1 and 7.6 mm Hg in study 2 at Week 48.
    81	
    82	
    83	 The most common adverse events were diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting, which occurred in approximately
    84	a quarter of patients taking tirzepatide. There were two adjudicated-confirmed cases of acute
    85	pancreatitis in those taking tirzepatide in study 2.
    86	
    87	
    88	 Patients who received tirzepatide also reported fewer daytime and nighttime disturbances, as
    89	measured using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form scale for
    90	Sleep-Related Impairment and Sleep Disturbance.
    91	
    92	
    93	 Tirzepatide Plus CPAP Are Best
    94	 Writing in an accompanying editorial, Sanjay R. Patel, MD, noted that although clinical guidelines
    95	have recommended that weight loss strategies be incorporated as part of OSA treatment, "the
    96	integration of obesity management into the approaches to care for obstructive sleep apnea has
    97	lagged."
    98	
    99	
   100	 As many as half of patients abandon CPAP therapy within 3 years, writes Patel, who is professor of
   101	medicine and epidemiology at the University of Pittsburgh, and medical director of the UPMC
   102	Comprehensive Sleep Disorders program. "An effective medication to treat obesity is thus an obvious
   103	avenue to pursue," he writes.
   104	
   105	
   106	 Patel noted the large reductions in the number of events on the AHI scale. He writes that the
   107	improvement in systolic blood pressure "was substantially larger than effects seen with CPAP therapy
   108	alone and indicate that tirzepatide may be an attractive option for those patients who seek to
   109	reduce their cardiovascular risk."
   110	
   111	
   112	 Patel raised concerns about whether patients outside of a trial would stick with therapy, noting
   113	studies have shown high rates of discontinuation of GLP-1 receptor agonists.
   114	
   115	
   116	 And, he writes, "Racial disparities in the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists among patients with
   117	diabetes arouse concern that the addition of tirzepatide as a treatment option for obstructive sleep
   118	apnea without directly addressing policies relative to coverage of care will only further exacerbate
   119	already pervasive disparities in clinical care for obstructive sleep apnea."
   120	
   121	
   122	 Commenting on the study during the presentation of the results, Louis Aronne, MD, said he believes
   123	the trials demonstrate "the treatment of obesity with tirzepatide plus CPAP is really the optimal
   124	treatment for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity-related cardiometabolic risks." Aronne is the
   125	Sanford I. Weill professor of metabolic research at Weill Cornell Medical College, New York.
   126	
   127	
   128	 Aronne added there is still much to learn. It is still not clear whether tirzepatide had an
   129	independent effect in the OSA trial — as has been seen in other studies where the drug clearly
   130	reduced cardiovascular risk — or whether the positive results were primarily due to weight loss.
   131	
   132	
   133	 "I believe that over time we'll see that this particular effect in sleep apnea is related to
   134	weight," he said.

The article in `doc.txt` describes tirzepatide as "the diabetes and weight loss drug tirzepatide (Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes; Zepbound for obesity)." The central connection between this medication and sleep apnea is that it "was so effective at reducing sleep disruptions in patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) that 40% to 50% no longer needed to use a continuous pressure airway positive (CPAP) device, according to two new studies."

**How the drug works.** The article identifies tirzepatide as "a long-acting glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist." Beyond that classification, the document does not describe a detailed physiological mechanism by which the drug opens the airway. Instead, it emphasizes that the drug "also lowered C-reactive protein levels and systolic blood pressure. And patients taking the medication lost 18% to 20% of their body weight."

**The weight-loss link.** The article explains why weight loss matters for OSA: "Obesity is a common risk factor. According to the ADA, 40% of those with obesity have OSA and 70% of those with OSA have obesity." The authors themselves acknowledge the uncertainty about the mechanism: "It is still not clear whether tirzepatide had an independent effect in the OSA trial — as has been seen in other studies where the drug clearly reduced cardiovascular risk — or whether the positive results were primarily due to weight loss." Louis Aronne added, "I believe that over time we'll see that this particular effect in sleep apnea is related to weight."

**The evidence.** The SURMOUNT-OSA studies were "two double-blind randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity and moderate-to-severe OSA" conducted "at 60 sites in nine countries," with results "presented here at the American Diabetes Association (ADA) 84th Scientific Sessions and simultaneously published online in the New England Journal of Medicine." Participants had "moderate-to-severe OSA, defined as more than 15 events per hour (using the apnea–hypopnea index [AHI]) and a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or greater." Those not using CPAP were enrolled in study 1, and those using CPAP in study 2. Participants received "either the maximum tolerated dose of tirzepatide (10 or 15 mg by once-weekly injection) or placebo for 1 year," along with lifestyle counseling.

**Results.** "At baseline, 65% to 70% of participants had severe OSA, with more than 30 events/hour on the AHI scale and a mean of 51.5 events/hour." "By 1 year, patients taking tirzepatide had 27 to 30 fewer events/hour compared with 4 to 6 fewer events/hour for those taking placebo." "Up to half of those who received tirzepatide in both trials had less than 5 events/hour or 5 to 14 AHI events/hour and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 10 or less. Those thresholds 'represent a level at which CPAP therapy may not be recommended,' write the authors."

**Benefits reported in the article:**
- Large reductions in apnea events and severity (27–30 fewer events/hour vs. 4–6 for placebo)
- 40% to 50% of patients no longer needing CPAP
- 18% to 20% body weight loss
- Decreased systolic blood pressure "from baseline of 9.7 mm Hg in study 1 and 7.6 mm Hg in study 2 at Week 48"
- Lowered C-reactive protein levels
- Patients "reported fewer daytime and nighttime disturbances"
- Sanjay R. Patel wrote that the blood pressure improvement "was substantially larger than effects seen with CPAP therapy alone and indicate that tirzepatide may be an attractive option for those patients who seek to reduce their cardiovascular risk."
- If it "eventually gain[s] US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for OSA, it would be the first drug approved for the condition," and it "offers a more accessible alternative for individuals who cannot tolerate or adhere to existing therapies."

**Caveats noted in the article.** The most common adverse events were "diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting, which occurred in approximately a quarter of patients taking tirzepatide. There were two adjudicated-confirmed cases of acute pancreatitis in those taking tirzepatide in study 2." Patel raised concerns about whether patients outside a trial would stick with therapy, "noting studies have shown high rates of discontinuation of GLP-1 receptor agonists," and about racial disparities in access. Finally, Aronne said he believes "the treatment of obesity with tirzepatide plus CPAP is really the optimal treatment for obstructive sleep apnea and obesity-related cardiometabolic risks."

In short, the document presents tirzepatide as a weight-loss and diabetes drug whose major benefit for sleep apnea appears to come largely through substantial weight loss, with the added effects of reduced apnea events, lower blood pressure, and reduced sleep disruption — though the article is explicit that it is not yet clear whether the drug has an independent effect on OSA beyond weight loss.
